items.title: Saturday 80s Jam: How Will I Know – Whitney Houston
items.author: Schill
items.content:
When Whitney Houston released “How Will I Know” in 1985, she was still in the early stages of what would become one of the most extraordinary careers in pop music. Her debut album had already produced “You Give Good Love,” but “How Will I Know” was the song that showed the world just how perfectly her enormous voice could fit into bright, energetic 1980s pop.

Written by George Merrill, Shannon Rubicam, and Narada Michael Walden, the song was originally intended for another artist. Houston’s version transformed it into something much bigger. Produced by Michael Walden, the recording combined synthesizers, electronic drums, handclaps, keyboards, and a relentlessly upbeat rhythm that was almost impossible to sit still through.

That was a major departure from the more serious image often associated with powerhouse vocalists.

Houston could obviously sing a huge ballad, but “How Will I Know” demonstrated that she could also have fun.

The song is essentially about romantic uncertainty. Houston is interested in someone but doesn’t know whether the feelings are mutual. Instead of treating that uncertainty as something dramatic and depressing, the song turns it into a burst of nervous energy.

The production is a huge part of that feeling.

The drums bounce along, the keyboards sparkle, the backing vocals reinforce the chorus, and Houston’s voice cuts through the arrangement with astonishing clarity. She doesn’t have to overpower the production. She simply sits perfectly on top of it.

Directed by Brian Grant, the “How Will I Know” video was filled with bright colors, geometric sets, dancers, energetic choreography, and unmistakable mid-1980s fashion. It was tailor-made for MTV, which was rapidly becoming one of the most important promotional forces in popular music.

Houston’s image in the video was youthful, stylish, and playful.

She wasn’t being presented solely as a serious vocalist standing behind a microphone. She was a pop star.

The song became Houston’s second number-one single on the Billboard Hot 100 and helped turn her debut album into a massive success. It also established a formula that would define much of her early career: combine an extraordinary voice with sophisticated pop production and make the result accessible to virtually anyone.

“How Will I Know” is particularly impressive because Houston never sounds like she’s struggling to fit into the upbeat production.

She sounds completely natural.

Her vocal runs add personality without overwhelming the melody, while the chorus gives her plenty of room to show off the power that would eventually become her trademark.

The song also captures something essential about 1980s pop. This was the decade when electronic production, MTV, fashion, dance music, and traditional vocal performances increasingly came together.

“How Will I Know” sits right in the middle of that cultural shift.

It sounds unmistakably like 1985, but its melody is strong enough that the song never feels trapped in its era.

Most importantly, it helped establish Whitney Houston as something more than a promising new singer.

She was becoming a superstar.

Over the next several years, Houston would deliver enormous ballads, blockbuster movie songs, and some of the most recognizable recordings in popular music.

But “How Will I Know” remains special because it captures her at the beginning of that journey.

Young, energetic, impossibly talented, and surrounded by one of the decade’s most infectious productions, Whitney Houston turned a song about wondering whether someone liked her into a celebration of the excitement of not knowing.

And the answer, judging by the success of the song, was pretty obvious.

Everybody was going to know Whitney Houston.

items.title: Forgotten Band: Icicle Works
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are plenty of forgotten bands from the 1980s that make you wonder how they ever disappeared. Then there are bands like The Icicle Works, where the question becomes even more frustrating:

How did a band this good have only one song that everybody remembers?

If you were listening to alternative radio in the early 1980s, you probably remember “Whisper to a Scream (Birds Fly).” It was catchy, energetic and just strange enough to stand apart from the endless parade of synth-heavy new wave that was filling radio stations.

The song was a legitimate hit.

And that’s a shame, because The Icicle Works had a much more interesting story than their one familiar song suggests.

They came from Liverpool, England, created a sound that mixed post-punk, new wave, progressive rock and straight-up pop, and produced several albums that deserve far more attention than they receive today.

They were never quite weird enough to be completely underground and never quite commercial enough to become superstars.

That awkward middle ground is where a lot of forgotten bands ended up.

From Liverpool to the World

The Icicle Works were formed in Liverpool in the early 1980s by singer, guitarist and songwriter Ian McNabb.

McNabb was the creative force behind the band, and his songwriting immediately separated The Icicle Works from many of their contemporaries.

The band wasn’t interested in simply copying the synth-pop formula.

There were keyboards and electronic textures, but there were also jangly guitars, driving rhythms and surprisingly ambitious arrangements.

The music could sound bright and upbeat while still having a slightly melancholy edge.

That combination fit perfectly into the early-1980s British alternative scene.

Liverpool already had a remarkable musical history, and The Icicle Works became part of another generation of musicians trying to figure out what came after punk.

The answer, for them, was to take the energy of punk and combine it with ambitious pop songwriting.

The song that changed everything was “Whisper to a Scream (Birds Fly).”

The title alone sounded like something you’d find printed on an early-’80s import single.

The song itself was even better.

It started with a distinctive rhythmic pulse before opening into jangling guitars and McNabb’s urgent vocals.

It was catchy without sounding disposable.

The song eventually became a significant hit in the United States, reaching the Top 40, and suddenly The Icicle Works had an opportunity to become much bigger.

For a brief moment, they looked like they might be one of the British bands capable of breaking through in America.

That didn’t quite happen.

Which is a shame, because they had the songs.

The band’s 1984 debut album, , is where anyone rediscovering the group should start.

It’s much more than a vehicle for “Whisper to a Scream.”

The album demonstrates just how adventurous McNabb could be as a songwriter.

There are atmospheric passages, energetic guitar-driven songs, electronic touches and big melodic choruses.

The band could shift from moody to explosive without losing its identity.

It’s very much an early-’80s record, but it doesn’t feel trapped in the decade.

That’s an important distinction.

A lot of new wave records now sound like museum pieces.

The Icicle Works still sounds like a band.

They Were More Than New Wave

Calling The Icicle Works a new wave band isn’t necessarily wrong, but it’s incomplete.

They had too many different influences.

There were progressive-rock ideas.

There was folk and psychedelic influence.

There were enormous pop melodies.

McNabb wasn’t afraid to experiment with song structures either.

That made the band difficult to categorize.

And once again, that’s probably part of the reason they never became huge.

The 1980s music industry loved easy descriptions.

The Icicle Works could fit into several of those categories without completely belonging to any of them.

The band continued with albums including and If You Want to Defeat Your Enemy Sing His Song.

The latter title alone should tell you something about McNabb.

He wasn’t exactly thinking in terms of three-minute radio formulas.

The albums continued to demonstrate that the band had plenty of ideas beyond their biggest American hit.

There were moments of experimentation alongside straightforward pop-rock.

Unfortunately, the commercial momentum wasn’t enough to turn The Icicle Works into a household name.

They became one of those bands that had a recognizable song without becoming a recognizable band.

That’s a particularly strange form of musical fame.

The Icicle Works benefited from MTV during the era when British bands were flooding American television.

The visual presentation of “Whisper to a Scream” helped the song stand out.

But MTV also created an interesting problem.

It could make a song famous much faster than it could make an entire catalog famous.

A viewer might see the video, remember the chorus, and move on to the next band.

That’s essentially what happened.

The Icicle Works became associated with one song.

The rest of the catalog disappeared behind it.

Ian McNabb Never Really Stopped

One of the biggest misconceptions about forgotten bands is that they disappeared because they had nothing left to say.

That wasn’t the case with Ian McNabb.

After The Icicle Works’ original run, McNabb continued recording and performing, including solo work and later incarnations of the band.

He remained an active musician while The Icicle Works became increasingly associated with nostalgia for the 1980s.

That’s another reason the group is worth rediscovering.

They’re not simply a historical curiosity.

There is a substantial body of music behind the one song most people remember.

The Icicle Works suffered from terrible timing.

They arrived during an extraordinary period in British music.

There were so many great bands that even genuinely talented groups could get lost.

You had The Cure, New Order, The Smiths, Echo & the Bunnymen, Simple Minds, U2, Tears for Fears, The Psychedelic Furs, The English Beat, The Church and dozens of others competing for attention.

That’s a ridiculous amount of competition.

A band could have a hit and still disappear from the larger cultural memory.

The Icicle Works did exactly that.

They became a footnote in a decade packed with musical stories.

The Great Thing About Rediscovering Them

The Icicle Works are one of those bands where the rediscovery process is genuinely rewarding.

You start with “Whisper to a Scream.”

You think, “Oh yeah, I remember this.”

Then you listen to the first album.

Wait a minute. These guys were actually really good.

And there are more songs.

More ambitious arrangements.

More of Ian McNabb’s excellent songwriting.

That’s the fun of forgotten bands.

You’re not discovering some obscure group that nobody liked.

You’re discovering a band that was good enough to have been much bigger but got lost in the shuffle.

They Deserve More Than One Song

The Icicle Works aren’t completely forgotten.

Their biggest song still turns up on ’80s playlists, radio retrospectives and new wave compilations.

But the band behind that song deserves to be remembered.

They weren’t a one-hit novelty.

They weren’t simply another synth-pop act.

They were a talented Liverpool band with a distinctive sound, a gifted songwriter and a willingness to experiment.

“Whisper to a Scream” may have been their ticket into the mainstream, but it shouldn’t be the end of the journey.

If that’s the only Icicle Works song you know, you’ve heard the introduction.

Now listen to the albums.

Because once you do, you’ll probably have the same reaction that happens with so many forgotten bands:

“How the hell did I forget these guys?”

And that might be the best reason of all to bring The Icicle Works back into the conversation.

They don’t need nostalgia.

They just need somebody to press play.

items.title: Humpday Hottie: Kaley Cuoco
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Kaley Cuoco is an American actress and producer best known for her work in television, particularly for playing Penny on the enormously successful sitcom . Born in Camarillo, California, in 1985, Cuoco began acting as a child and appeared in commercials and television programs before landing roles that established her as a recognizable young performer.

Her early breakthrough came with the sitcom , where she played Bridget Hennessy. The series gave Cuoco significant exposure and helped establish her as a talented comedic actress. She later joined the cast of during its final season, expanding her television résumé.

Her biggest success arrived in 2007 when premiered. Cuoco played Penny, an aspiring actress and waitress who moves into an apartment across the hall from physicists Leonard Hofstadter and Sheldon Cooper. Penny’s personality provided an important contrast to the show’s highly intellectual characters, and Cuoco became one of the central performers in the series. The show ultimately ran for 12 seasons and became one of television’s most successful sitcoms.

After , Cuoco demonstrated a different side of her acting abilities in the HBO Max series . She played Cassie Bowden, a flight attendant whose life becomes complicated after she wakes up beside a dead passenger. The series combined comedy, mystery, and drama, earning Cuoco multiple award nominations.

Cuoco has also worked extensively as a producer through her company, Yes, Norman Productions. She has continued appearing in film and television while developing projects behind the scenes.

With her combination of comedic timing, dramatic range, and production experience, Cuoco has successfully moved beyond the sitcom role that made her famous. Her career has evolved from child performer to sitcom star and ultimately to an established actress and producer with a diverse body of work.

items.title: Troma Tuesday: Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are movies that are difficult to explain.

Then there are movies like Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters, where explaining the plot might actually make the movie sound less believable than simply watching it.

Released in 1982, this bizarre Troma release is an American reworking of the Indonesian action film . Directed by Jopi Burnama with Charles Kaufman involved in the Troma version, the movie takes Indonesian martial-arts and wrestling footage, strips away the original soundtrack and adds a completely new English-language comedic dub. The result is part action movie, part exploitation film and part drunken midnight-movie commentary track.

In other words, exactly the sort of thing Troma would distribute.

The basic story actually sounds reasonably serious.

Bambi, played by Indonesian action star Eva Arnaz, is a former judo champion who wants to get away from the fighting business. Unfortunately, her family needs money. Her younger brother requires an expensive operation, leaving Bambi with very few options. She eventually gets involved with a female wrestling operation, which pulls her into a world involving shady characters, violence and criminal activity.

That sounds like the setup for a gritty Indonesian martial-arts drama.

And then Troma got hold of it.

The American version is essentially a giant joke built around footage that was originally intended to be taken much more seriously. The dialogue was redubbed, the tone was transformed and the movie was presented as a bizarre comedy. The American version runs roughly 74 minutes, considerably shorter than the original Indonesian version, which has also been released under titles including .

This is where Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters becomes fascinating.

The actual action footage is frequently pretty impressive.

Eva Arnaz was a genuine Indonesian action star, and the original production gives her plenty to do. There are martial-arts sequences, wrestling matches, fights and criminal-syndicate shenanigans. The movie comes from an era of Indonesian exploitation cinema when filmmakers were producing wildly energetic genre movies with a mixture of martial arts, melodrama, horror and adventure.

Troma looks at all of that and essentially says:

“Yeah, but what if everyone sounded completely ridiculous?”

The redubbing is the star of the American version.

Instead of trying to create a convincing English-language adaptation, the new dialogue goes straight for absurdity. Characters suddenly sound like they’re participating in an entirely different movie. Serious scenes become jokes. Dramatic confrontations become opportunities for ridiculous dialogue.

It’s basically after somebody replaced Woody Allen with the Troma crew.

And the weirdness doesn’t stop there.

One of the movie’s most famously ridiculous plot points involves Bambi’s brother and an extraordinarily strange medical condition that supposedly requires an operation. The premise is so completely bonkers that attempting to discuss it seriously feels like a waste of everyone’s time.

Then there is Barry Prima, another major Indonesian action star, playing Barney. In a normal version of the movie, his character is a martial-arts figure involved in Bambi’s increasingly complicated situation. In the Troma version, he becomes part of the lunacy, with the dubbing turning him into one of the movie’s many sources of comic absurdity.

What makes the whole thing work is the contrast.

You have serious-looking action footage.

You have beautiful Indonesian locations.

You have actors who clearly know how to perform martial arts.

You have dramatic music and editing from the original production.

And over the top of all of it, you have dialogue that sounds like it was written by people who had absolutely no intention of respecting the source material.

The movie is also very much a product of Troma’s early-’80s philosophy. Troma didn’t necessarily need every film it handled to be technically polished. It needed personality.

And Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters has personality coming out of every available hole.

The biggest problem is that the joke can become repetitive. Once you understand what Troma has done, the basic formula doesn’t change much. Serious scene appears. Ridiculous dialogue arrives. Fight happens. More ridiculous dialogue follows.

Eventually, you know exactly what the movie is going to do.

But then something completely insane happens anyway.

That unpredictability keeps it alive.

The movie also benefits from being short. At around 74 minutes in its American re-edited form, it doesn’t have much time to become boring.

Because this is not a movie you watch for character development.

You’re not emotionally invested in Bambi’s journey because you’ve spent three hours getting to know her.

You’re here for the fights.

You’re here for the dubbing.

You’re here for the sheer audacity of taking a relatively straightforward Indonesian action film and transforming it into something that feels like an entirely different genre.

The film is also an interesting reminder of how strange the international exploitation business could be before streaming made practically every movie in the world accessible from a laptop.

Troma’s version effectively created a new movie out of an existing one. The original was an Indonesian action drama, while Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters became an American cult comedy through editing and dubbing.

Today, that concept might sound familiar, but in the context of Troma’s catalog it fits perfectly.

It’s a movie that exists because somebody looked at perfectly usable martial-arts footage and thought it would be much funnier if everyone suddenly started saying ridiculous things.

The strangest thing about Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters is that underneath all the Troma nonsense, there’s a legitimate action movie struggling to escape.

Eva Arnaz is charismatic.

The fight scenes have genuine energy.

The Indonesian setting gives the movie a visual identity that most low-budget American exploitation movies simply couldn’t duplicate.

Then the dubbing comes crashing through the door and starts throwing pies at everything.

That’s the entire experience.

If you’re expecting a serious martial-arts movie, you’ll probably be confused.

If you’re expecting a conventional comedy, you’ll probably be confused.

If you’re expecting Troma to take something completely straight-faced and turn it into a deranged midnight movie, you’re exactly where you need to be.

Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters isn’t necessarily a great movie.

But it is a .

It’s bizarre, cheap, energetic, occasionally offensive, frequently hilarious and completely incapable of behaving like a normal film.

And honestly, that’s why it remains memorable.

The movie doesn’t simply break the fourth wall.

It grabs the fourth wall, throws it into a wrestling ring and starts beating it with a folding chair.

Ferocious Female Freedom Fighters is exactly the kind of cinematic lunacy that makes cult-movie hunting worthwhile. The original Indonesian action footage is entertaining on its own, but Troma’s completely ridiculous redubbing turns it into something much stranger.

It’s not a movie you watch because you need a coherent story.

It’s a movie you watch because you want to see how badly someone can derail a perfectly respectable martial-arts film.

Just don’t expect the title to be the strangest thing about it.

items.title: Song Battle: The Jim Carroll Band – “People Who Died” vs Nails “88 Lines About 44 Women”
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Two songs. Two bands. Two very different ways of turning a list of troubled lives into unforgettable rock songs.

The Jim Carroll Band’s “People Who Died” and The Nails’ “88 Lines About 44 Women” are both unusual pieces of late-1970s/early-1980s rock songwriting. Neither follows the traditional formula of telling one straightforward story. Instead, both songs pile up names, characters, memories and fragments until the sheer accumulation becomes the point.

“People Who Died” is loud, fast and furious. Jim Carroll races through a list of people from his past who died young, turning grief into something that sounds almost celebratory. The music barrels forward while Carroll delivers one name after another.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” takes the opposite approach. The Nails strip the music down and let Doug Bowles deliver a surreal catalog of women, each described in a few words or phrases. The song feels detached, mysterious and strangely hypnotic.

One is a punk-rock memorial.

The other is a bizarre character gallery.

One makes death sound like a reason to turn the volume up.

The other makes you wonder who the hell all these people are.

Both are brilliantly unconventional.

Song Profile: “People Who Died”

Released in 1980 on , “People Who Died” became Jim Carroll’s signature song and one of the most distinctive pieces of punk-influenced rock songwriting of its era.

Carroll was already known as a poet and writer before making the record, and that background is obvious. The song doesn’t unfold like a conventional rock narrative. Instead, Carroll remembers people from his life who died, moving rapidly from one story to another.

The lyrics are packed with specific names and details, but the song never becomes a solemn memorial.

Carroll sings with urgency while the band drives the song forward with punk energy. The result is strangely uplifting despite being built almost entirely around death.

There is grief underneath it, but there is also affection, humor and the sense that remembering these people is a way of keeping them alive.

The song feels like someone opening an old address book and discovering that far too many names are gone.

And then turning that realization into a rock song.

Song Profile: “88 Lines About 44 Women”

The Nails’ “88 Lines About 44 Women” appeared in 1981 and became the band’s best-known song.

Where “People Who Died” moves at punk-rock speed, “88 Lines” is deliberately restrained.

The concept is simple but unusual: 44 women are described in two lines each.

There is no traditional narrative connecting them. Instead, the listener gets fragments of personalities, relationships, occupations, lifestyles and strange little details.

The song’s delivery is almost spoken rather than conventionally sung.

If it were performed as a conventional rock song, much of the mystery would disappear. Instead, The Nails make the listener feel like they’re overhearing someone tell stories about dozens of people they may or may not actually know.

The song is funny, strange, occasionally dark and endlessly quotable.

And somehow, despite having 44 separate characters, it never feels like homework.

Both songs are built around unconventional concepts.

“People Who Died” takes what could have been a depressing list of names and turns it into a coherent rock song with momentum, emotional progression and a memorable refrain.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” is arguably even more unusual. The entire song is based on a mathematical structure: 44 women, two lines apiece.

But “People Who Died” has more musical and emotional development.

The list isn’t just a gimmick.

Every name contributes to the larger feeling of memory, mortality and loss.

Jim Carroll takes the opening round.

This is an incredibly difficult category.

Carroll’s writing is direct but packed with personality. Each person mentioned feels like they had a life beyond the few seconds they occupy in the song.

The Nails go in a completely different direction.

“88 Lines” is almost literary in its construction. Each couplet creates another character and another unanswered question.

Why these particular details?

The mystery becomes part of the appeal.

But Carroll’s lyrics have greater emotional impact.

The Jim Carroll Band takes another round.

Jim Carroll sounds like he’s trying to outrun the memories.

His vocal is energetic, rough around the edges and filled with urgency. He doesn’t sound like a polished rock singer, which makes the song feel more personal.

The Nails’ vocal approach is completely different.

The detached delivery of “88 Lines” is one of its greatest strengths. It almost sounds like someone reading from a notebook at three in the morning.

But Carroll’s performance demands more.

There’s excitement, sadness, anger and affection packed into the delivery.

Carroll wins the vocal battle.

Round 4: Musical Arrangement

“People Who Died” is a full-on band performance.

The guitars, drums and bass create a driving punk-rock foundation that gives Carroll’s list of names an almost unstoppable momentum.

The Nails deliberately keep things sparse.

That works beautifully for “88 Lines,” because the arrangement leaves space for the words to dominate.

But if we’re judging the overall musical arrangement rather than minimalism itself, “People Who Died” has more impact.

The Jim Carroll Band goes up 4–0.

Now The Nails get their revenge.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” is one of the strangest concepts to become a legitimate rock hit.

No traditional narrative.

Just a succession of increasingly bizarre characters.

“People Who Died” is also highly original, but songs built around lists of names and memories have a long history.

The Nails created something that feels almost impossible to categorize.

Winner: 88 Lines About 44 Women

The Nails finally get on the board.

“People Who Died” is ridiculously catchy.

The rhythm is immediate, the repeated title becomes a hook and the song’s structure makes it easy to anticipate what comes next.

You hear it once and the central refrain can stay in your head for hours.

“88 Lines” is catchy in a completely different way.

Its melody is memorable, but the real hook is the accumulation of the characters.

You remember the concept.

You remember the delivery.

But “People Who Died” is the one you’re more likely to find yourself singing.

Round 7: Character & Personality

This is where “88 Lines About 44 Women” becomes almost impossible to beat.

The song is basically a collection of characters.

Each woman gets a tiny portrait, and each portrait gives you just enough information to imagine an entire story.

Some seem completely ordinary.

The genius is knowing when to stop.

The Nails never explain everything.

They just give you enough to make you curious.

“People Who Died” also contains memorable personalities, but its focus is the narrator’s relationship to those people rather than the characters themselves.

Winner: 88 Lines About 44 Women

The Nails even the score at 4–3.

Round 8: Emotional Impact

“88 Lines” is fascinating.

Underneath the speed and punk energy, Carroll is singing about people who were once part of his world and are no longer here.

That makes it even more powerful.

There’s something incredibly human about the way Carroll moves through the names, refusing to let the song become a funeral.

Instead, the memories become the celebration.

The Jim Carroll Band pulls ahead again.

The Nails have the advantage here.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” creates a strange, late-night atmosphere that is difficult to duplicate.

The sparse instrumentation and almost spoken delivery make the song feel like you’re listening to somebody reveal secrets.

It has a smoky barroom quality without actually sounding like a traditional bar song.

“People Who Died” is much more immediate.

It’s loud, fast and energetic.

But “88 Lines” creates a world.

Winner: 88 Lines About 44 Women

Round 10: Cultural Impact

“People Who Died” became Jim Carroll’s signature song.

It has been covered, referenced and repeatedly rediscovered by new generations of listeners. Its unusual combination of punk energy, poetry and personal history makes it one of the most recognizable songs of its type.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” had a similar effect for The Nails.

The song became their defining recording and remains one of the most distinctive songs of the early new-wave era.

But “People Who Died” has endured particularly well because its subject is universal.

Everyone eventually knows people who are gone.

That makes the song’s central idea almost impossible to date.

Jim Carroll takes the lead, 5–5.

Everything comes down to the final round.

Round 11: The Tiebreaker — Which Is the Better Song?

This is where the battle gets decided.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” is arguably the more unusual song.

Its concept is brilliant, its atmosphere is unforgettable and its characters practically demand that you invent stories about them.

But “People Who Died” has the thing that ultimately separates a great concept from a great song:

The list of names isn’t simply clever.

Carroll turns memory into momentum. The band makes grief sound exciting. The song moves so quickly that you barely have time to process each person before another name arrives.

And that is precisely what makes it work.

Life doesn’t stop because someone dies.

And the people who are gone remain alive in your memories.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” makes you curious.

“People Who Died” makes you feel something.

People Who Died — 6 rounds

88 Lines About 44 Women — 5 rounds

The Winner: “People Who Died”

The Jim Carroll Band wins a battle that was much closer than the final score suggests.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” is an extraordinary piece of songwriting. The concept is almost absurdly simple, yet The Nails turn it into something memorable, strange and hypnotic. It remains one of the most original songs to come out of the new-wave era.

But “People Who Died” has a deeper emotional punch.

Jim Carroll takes a list of dead friends, acquaintances and people from his past and refuses to turn them into statistics. Every name represents a life.

The song is sad without being miserable.

It’s angry without being bitter.

And somehow, it’s even fun.

That’s an incredible trick.

The Nails give us 44 mysteries.

Jim Carroll gives us memories.

“88 Lines About 44 Women” is the more unusual song.

“People Who Died” is the more powerful one.

And when the final round asks which song you’d still want to hear decades later, with the volume turned all the way up, the answer is Jim Carroll.

Winner: The Jim Carroll Band — “People Who Died”

items.title: Saturday 80s Jam: Faith – George Michael
items.author: Schill
items.content:
When George Michael released “Faith” in 1987, he was already one of the biggest pop stars on the planet. But the song represented something much more significant than another hit single. It was the moment Michael stepped completely out of the shadow of Wham! and established himself as a solo artist with his own identity, sound, and image.

The title track from his debut solo album, , was almost deceptively simple. Built around a stripped-down acoustic guitar riff, handclaps, percussion, and Michael’s confident vocal, the song sounded dramatically different from the polished synth-pop that had helped make Wham! famous.

Michael wanted to move in a more mature musical direction, drawing on rockabilly, early rock ‘n’ roll, soul, and R&B. “Faith” combined those influences into something that sounded both retro and completely suited to 1987.

The opening is particularly memorable. The church-organ sound fades into the guitar riff before Michael enters, creating an unusual mixture of gospel imagery and rock ‘n’ roll swagger. The song then settles into a deceptively relaxed groove.

Michael wasn’t simply singing about romantic faith. The song is also about independence and refusing to remain trapped in a relationship that isn’t working.

That attitude was reflected in the video, which became one of the most recognizable pieces of MTV-era imagery. Michael appeared in leather, sunglasses, blue jeans, and a leather jacket, playing guitar in front of a jukebox.

The image was a complete transformation from the carefully coordinated pop-star presentation associated with Wham!

The transformation worked.

“Faith” became a massive commercial success, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in the United States. The album became one of the biggest-selling records of the decade, eventually earning Michael the Grammy Award for Album of the Year.

The song itself became one of the defining singles of 1987.

What made it particularly impressive was how little it actually needed. There wasn’t a giant synthesizer arrangement or an enormous chorus. The hook came from the rhythm, the guitar, Michael’s personality, and the confidence of the performance.

He sounded completely in control.

That confidence was important because “Faith” arrived during one of the most significant transitions of Michael’s career. Wham! had been enormously successful, but remaining part of a duo would always make it difficult for Michael to establish exactly who he was as an artist.

With , he didn’t simply continue what Wham! had started.

The song also demonstrated Michael’s extraordinary ability to move between musical styles. He could write sophisticated pop songs, soulful ballads, dance tracks, and more stripped-down rock-influenced material without sounding like he was simply copying someone else.

“Faith” became the perfect introduction to that new version of George Michael.

More than anything, the song is memorable because it feels effortless. The guitar riff is simple. The arrangement is relatively sparse. The rhythm is straightforward.

But getting simplicity to sound this good is difficult.

Every element is in exactly the right place.

The result was a song that managed to sound retro, modern, sexy, playful, and confident all at once.

Nearly four decades later, “Faith” remains one of George Michael’s defining recordings. It marked the beginning of one of the most successful solo careers of the late 1980s and proved that Michael was capable of becoming something beyond the pop star audiences already knew.

Wham! had made George Michael famous.

“Faith” made it clear that George Michael didn’t need Wham! anymore.

items.title: Empire Records: The Beautiful Genius of a Movie That Understood Being Young
items.author: Schill
items.content:
** I’m not going to bury the lead here.  Youtube Movies currently has Empire Records available to stream for free. So here it is, if you don’t want to read the article I spent an hour writing, have at it **

Now if you actually wanna read it……..

Some movies capture a moment in time so perfectly that they become more than entertainment. They become time capsules, preserving the music, fashion, attitudes, anxieties, and absurd little details of a generation. is one of those movies. Released in 1995, it arrived with an unassuming story about a group of record store employees trying to save their workplace, but beneath its modest premise was something much more meaningful: a celebration of individuality, friendship, music, and the terrifying, exhilarating experience of figuring out who you are.

At the box office, didn’t exactly set the world on fire. Critics were largely unimpressed, and the movie initially struggled to find an audience. Yet over the years, it developed a devoted following, particularly among people who recognized themselves in its collection of outsiders, misfits, music obsessives, and young adults who hadn’t quite figured out what they wanted from life.

Its enduring appeal isn’t an accident. The genius of lies in its understanding that growing up rarely happens through grand revelations. Sometimes it happens during an awful shift at work, an argument with a friend, a terrible decision made at two in the morning, or a conversation with someone who understands you better than you understand yourself.

And sometimes, it happens in a record store.

A Simple Story With Something Bigger at Its Heart

The premise of is deceptively straightforward. The employees of an independent record store discover that their beloved workplace is in danger of being absorbed into a corporate chain. Over the course of a chaotic day, they navigate personal problems, romantic entanglements, musical ambitions, financial disasters, and the usual assortment of teenage catastrophes.

On paper, this sounds like the foundation for a conventional workplace comedy. In practice, the record store becomes a miniature world where each character represents a different struggle with identity, insecurity, ambition, or belonging.

The store isn’t merely where the characters work. It’s where they spend their lives, where they find their friends, and where they feel most comfortable being themselves. It provides a refuge from parents, school, social expectations, and the increasingly complicated business of becoming an adult.

That distinction matters. For many young people, a first job is simply a way to earn money. But occasionally, a workplace becomes a community. The people behind the counter become your friends. The customers become familiar faces. The music playing through the speakers becomes the soundtrack to an entire chapter of your life.

understands that emotional connection. The store is imperfect, financially precarious, and occasionally ridiculous, but it belongs to the people who inhabit it.

The looming corporate takeover threatens more than a business. It threatens the characters’ sense of home.

That’s what gives the story its emotional foundation. Saving Empire Records becomes a way of protecting the world they’ve built together.

The Characters Feel Like People You Actually Knew

One of the movie’s greatest strengths is its ensemble cast. Rather than building the entire story around one protagonist, distributes its emotional weight across a collection of young people whose personalities, problems, and ambitions collide throughout the film.

They’re exaggerated enough to be entertaining but recognizable enough to feel real.

There’s Lucas, the impulsive employee whose attempt to save the store through a reckless gamble creates the crisis that drives the story. There’s Corey, the academically gifted overachiever whose carefully managed life begins to unravel under the pressure of expectations. Gina is confident, provocative, and determined to be taken seriously, even when she isn’t entirely sure what she wants.

Debra is withdrawn and angry, carrying pain that her coworkers don’t fully understand. A.J. is an aspiring artist caught between romantic feelings and the uncertainty of pursuing a creative life. Warren, meanwhile, arrives as an outsider and quickly becomes part of the store’s increasingly chaotic orbit.

Then there’s Mark, whose laid-back, slightly ridiculous personality provides some of the film’s funniest moments.

What makes these characters work is that none of them has everything figured out. They possess different degrees of confidence, intelligence, sensitivity, and self-awareness, but they’re all struggling with something.

Corey might look like the person most likely to succeed, but academic achievement doesn’t protect her from insecurity. Gina’s boldness doesn’t eliminate her need for validation. A.J.’s artistic ambitions don’t make difficult conversations any easier. Debra’s anger doesn’t tell the whole story of what she’s experiencing.

These contradictions make the characters interesting.

The movie doesn’t suggest that being young automatically makes someone profound or that every problem can be solved with a heartfelt speech. Instead, it presents a group of people who are frequently immature, selfish, confused, and occasionally wonderful.

In other words, they’re believable.

The genius is in allowing their personalities to clash without making every disagreement a moral lesson. They’re coworkers, friends, potential lovers, and occasional irritants. They don’t always understand one another, but their lives overlap enough that they gradually learn to care.

For anyone who worked a job in their teens or early twenties, the dynamic feels remarkably familiar. There was always a Lucas, a Gina, a Corey, or a Mark somewhere in the building. There were friendships that made no sense on paper but worked perfectly in practice.

And there was almost always someone who made an ordinary shift memorable.

The Record Store Is the Real Star

Although the characters carry the story, Empire Records itself is arguably the movie’s most important creation.

The store represents a particular kind of cultural space that has become increasingly difficult to find. It’s a place where music is something you discover rather than something an algorithm delivers to you. You browse without necessarily knowing what you’re looking for. You pick up an album because the cover catches your eye. You ask an employee for a recommendation and end up discovering a band that changes your life.

Music is personal in this environment. It isn’t simply background entertainment. It’s a way of expressing identity, finding community, and communicating feelings that are otherwise difficult to articulate.

The employees understand this instinctively. Their musical interests help define who they are, and the store allows them to share those interests with one another.

The movie also recognizes the social importance of independent businesses. Empire Records isn’t just competing on price or convenience. Its value comes from its personality, its employees, and the feeling that the place belongs to its community.

A corporate chain might offer a more efficient business model, but efficiency isn’t the same thing as character.

That conflict gives the film an unexpectedly enduring theme. The struggle between independent culture and corporate consolidation wasn’t invented in the 1990s, and it certainly hasn’t disappeared. It applies to record stores, bookstores, music venues, movie theaters, and countless other places where the personality of a business is inseparable from the people who make it special.

The film doesn’t need to deliver a lecture about capitalism to make its point. It shows us what would be lost if Empire Records disappeared.

We understand why these characters care because we’ve spent time inside their world.

And that is much more effective than simply telling the audience that independent stores are important.

The Soundtrack Is Practically Another Character

Any discussion of that doesn’t give its soundtrack considerable attention is missing a major part of the movie’s identity.

Music isn’t merely placed between scenes to keep the energy moving. It establishes the atmosphere, reveals character, and helps turn the store into a believable cultural universe.

The soundtrack captures the alternative-rock sensibility of the mid-1990s, when grunge was still influencing popular culture, Britpop was finding a wider audience, and alternative music had become a dominant force among young listeners.

The film’s musical selections create a recognizable sense of time without making the experience feel like a history lesson.

Among the standout songs is the Gin Blossoms’ “Til I Hear It from You,” which became closely associated with the movie and reached a much wider audience through its connection to the film. The song captures the restless romantic energy of the story while fitting naturally into its broader musical identity.

Then there’s the inclusion of “Sugarhigh” by Coyote Shivers, a perfect example of the movie’s willingness to embrace playful, slightly chaotic rock-and-roll energy.

The soundtrack also benefits from the presence of artists such as The Cranberries, Better Than Ezra, and other performers associated with the alternative scene of the era. Together, they create an environment that feels lived in rather than artificially assembled.

But the soundtrack’s real achievement is how naturally it connects music with personality.

The characters don’t just happen to work in a record store. They’re people for whom music is part of the language they use to understand the world. Their tastes, attitudes, and emotional responses are shaped by the songs surrounding them.

For audiences who grew up during the period, the music can trigger an almost physical sense of nostalgia. A song begins, and suddenly you’re remembering the clothes you wore, the people you knew, the places you went, and the albums you played until you practically wore them out.

For younger viewers, the soundtrack offers a window into a time when discovering music often required a little more curiosity and a lot more wandering through record-store racks.

The film’s musical identity is so strong that it would be difficult to imagine it working nearly as well without it.

The songs don’t simply accompany the story.

A Movie About Being Young Without Knowing What Comes Next

Beneath the comedy, romance, and musical nostalgia, is fundamentally a story about uncertainty.

The characters are standing at the edge of adulthood, but none of them has received a reliable instruction manual. They have ambitions, expectations, insecurities, and romantic fantasies, but the future remains frustratingly unclear.

Corey is trying to meet expectations that may not even reflect what she truly wants. A.J. is wrestling with the vulnerability required to pursue his artistic ambitions and express his feelings. Gina is trying to reconcile the person she presents to the world with the person she wants to become.

Debra’s struggles are more serious, giving the film an emotional dimension that extends beyond ordinary teenage confusion.

These stories work because the movie understands that growing up isn’t a clean transition from ignorance to wisdom. It’s a process of making mistakes, recognizing your limitations, and occasionally discovering that the life you thought you wanted isn’t necessarily the life that will make you happy.

The characters don’t suddenly become adults by the end of the movie. They’re still young, still impulsive, and still capable of making terrible decisions.

What changes is their understanding of themselves and one another.

They begin to recognize that the people around them are dealing with problems that aren’t always visible. Someone who appears confident may be desperately insecure. Someone who seems detached may be hurting. Someone who appears to have a perfect future may be terrified of it.

That recognition creates empathy.

And empathy, rather than maturity in the conventional sense, becomes one of the movie’s most important ideas.

The film suggests that growing up involves learning to see other people more clearly, even when you haven’t quite figured yourself out.

The Genius of Its Imperfect Tone

One reason has remained such a divisive movie is that its tone can be all over the place.

It moves between broad comedy, romantic awkwardness, workplace chaos, emotional drama, and moments of genuine sadness. Some scenes are deliberately ridiculous. Others are surprisingly sincere. Occasionally, the movie shifts from one emotional register to another so quickly that it feels as though several different films are competing for the same running time.

Its characters can be cartoonish. Some of its conflicts are resolved with a convenience that real life rarely provides. Certain moments lean heavily into the heightened emotional style of 1990s youth cinema.

These are legitimate weaknesses.

Yet the same qualities contribute to the film’s personality.

feels messy because its characters are messy. Its emotional shifts reflect the intensity with which young people can experience life, when a disastrous afternoon feels like the end of the world and a great night with friends feels like the beginning of everything.

The movie doesn’t always know when to be subtle, but it understands the emotional scale of being young.

At that age, you can experience embarrassment, heartbreak, excitement, anger, and joy within the space of a single day. A minor humiliation can feel catastrophic. A romantic gesture can seem monumental. A friendship can become the most important thing in your life.

The film captures that intensity through its restless pacing and occasionally excessive sentimentality.

Its rough edges also prevent it from feeling too polished or corporate. There’s an appealing scruffiness to the whole enterprise, an impression that the movie is more interested in its characters than in maintaining perfect narrative discipline.

Not every scene lands. Not every joke works. Not every character receives the development they deserve.

But the movie has a pulse.

And sometimes, personality is more valuable than perfection.

Why the Movie Became a Cult Classic

The history of is part of what makes its legacy so interesting.

The movie was not initially received as the generational touchstone it would eventually become. Its theatrical performance was disappointing, and its reputation grew through later viewings, home video, cable television, and the gradual accumulation of devoted fans.

That evolution reflects something important about the way audiences connect with movies.

A film can fail to make an immediate impression and still find the right people at the right time. Sometimes a movie’s most important audience isn’t the one that sees it on opening weekend. It’s the audience that discovers it years later, when the characters’ experiences suddenly feel personal.

For many viewers, became a movie associated with a particular period of life. They watched it with friends, quoted its dialogue, memorized its soundtrack, and returned to it whenever they wanted to revisit the atmosphere of the 1990s.

The film also benefited from the strength of its central setting. A record store is a remarkably effective place to build a coming-of-age story because it brings together people with different personalities while giving them a shared interest.

The characters have somewhere to go, something to do, and a reason to spend time together. Their lives intersect naturally, without requiring the plot to manufacture an elaborate excuse for every encounter.

That makes the movie easy to revisit. Even when viewers know exactly how the story unfolds, they can return simply to spend time with the characters.

This is one of the defining qualities of a cult classic: the pleasure isn’t limited to discovering what happens next. It’s about returning to a world you enjoy inhabiting.

The movie’s cultural afterlife has also been sustained by the music, the fashion, the dialogue, and its association with an era that now feels both familiar and distant.

For those who experienced the 1990s firsthand, it offers a concentrated dose of nostalgia. For viewers who came later, it provides an appealing portrait of a pre-streaming music culture built around physical spaces, shared discoveries, and personal recommendations.

Its imperfections haven’t prevented it from becoming beloved.

In some ways, they’ve helped.

The Movie Understands the Importance of Finding Your People

Perhaps the most emotionally resonant element of is its belief that people don’t have to be perfect to matter to one another.

The employees are an unlikely collection of personalities. They don’t always agree, and they certainly don’t always behave well. They make impulsive decisions, hurt one another’s feelings, and occasionally create problems that would be easier to solve if everyone simply acted like a reasonable adult.

But they keep showing up.

They share a workplace, a passion for music, and an increasingly urgent reason to work together. Over time, those connections become more meaningful than their differences.

The film’s emotional payoff depends on the audience believing that this group of people genuinely cares about one another. Their efforts to save the store become a collective expression of loyalty, not merely an attempt to preserve their jobs.

This is an important distinction.

A workplace can be replaceable. A community is harder to reproduce.

The characters are fighting for something that gives their lives structure and meaning. They’re protecting the place where they belong, even if they haven’t fully recognized how important that belonging is until it comes under threat.

That idea extends far beyond the movie’s setting.

Almost everyone has experienced a period in life when a group of friends, a favorite hangout, a workplace, or a shared interest becomes the center of their social universe. At the time, it may feel completely ordinary. Only later do you realize how much those experiences shaped you.

captures that feeling before nostalgia has a chance to soften it.

The characters aren’t looking back on their youth. They’re living it, with all the confusion and immediacy that entails.

That’s why the movie’s friendships feel so appealing. They’re not presented as perfect relationships between idealized people. They’re relationships between individuals who are still learning how to care for one another.

The store gives them a place to begin.

A Time Capsule of a World That Has Changed

Watching today means encountering a version of music culture that has largely disappeared.

The physical record store was once a central destination for people who loved music. New releases generated excitement. Album covers were objects to examine. Listening to a record involved a physical purchase, and discovering a new artist could be the result of browsing shelves for an hour.

The internet eventually transformed that experience, followed by digital downloads and streaming services. Music became more accessible than ever, but the process of finding it changed dramatically.

Today, someone can explore an enormous catalog without leaving home. Recommendations can be generated automatically, and entire discographies are available with a few taps.

Those conveniences are extraordinary. Yet they also make the particular environment of feel increasingly special.

The store represents a time when discovering music was often a social experience. You talked to employees, argued about bands, compared albums, and occasionally bought something simply because a friend insisted that you had to hear it.

The experience involved chance, conversation, and physical presence.

The movie doesn’t need to claim that the past was universally better. It simply reminds us that something valuable existed in that older culture, something that couldn’t be measured entirely in sales figures or streaming numbers.

The record store was a place where people could gather around a shared passion without needing to agree on everything else.

That spirit remains relevant even as the physical setting changes. Independent music venues, local bookstores, record shops, fan communities, and other cultural spaces continue to provide opportunities for people to connect through the things they love.

The world of may be rooted in 1995, but its underlying idea isn’t tied to a particular decade.

People still need places where they feel welcome.

They still need music that makes them feel understood.

And they still need friends who will help them get through the days when everything seems to be going wrong.

The Performances That Make It Work

The movie’s ensemble is essential to its lasting appeal, and its cast deserves credit for creating characters who remain memorable even when the script occasionally pushes them toward caricature.

Rory Cochrane gives Lucas an appealing mixture of intelligence, recklessness, and desperation. He’s the kind of person who can convince himself that an increasingly terrible decision is actually a brilliant plan, right up until the consequences arrive.

Liv Tyler brings vulnerability to Corey, making her more than the familiar high-achieving student whose private life doesn’t match her public image. Her performance helps ground a character whose anxieties could otherwise feel like a collection of familiar coming-of-age tropes.

Renée Zellweger gives Gina a brash, funny confidence that masks a more complicated desire to be taken seriously. The character can be frustrating, but Zellweger makes her difficult to dismiss.

Robin Tunney’s Debra provides some of the film’s most affecting moments. She conveys a guardedness that makes the character’s emotional struggles feel distinct from the lighter problems surrounding her. The performance adds weight to a movie that could easily have treated every difficulty as another opportunity for comedy.

Johnny Whitworth gives A.J. an understated awkwardness that works well against the louder personalities around him, while Ethan Embry’s Mark supplies a steady stream of eccentricity.

The supporting cast helps establish the sense that Empire Records exists beyond the boundaries of the main storyline. These characters have personalities and histories that the movie only partially explores, which makes the world feel larger than the plot itself.

That’s another reason the film remains enjoyable. It gives viewers enough information to understand the characters while leaving room for the imagination to fill in the rest.

You can easily picture what these people might have been doing before the movie began or where their lives might take them afterward.

The film’s greatest achievement isn’t that every character is fully developed. It’s that so many of them feel like people whose stories could continue after the credits roll.

Why Still Matters

The genius of isn’t that it is a flawless movie. It isn’t.

Its plotting can be contrived, its tone occasionally wanders, and its characters sometimes behave in ways that seem designed to move the story forward rather than reflect real human behavior. It wears its heart on its sleeve, and there are moments when that sentimentality becomes a little overwhelming.

But the film possesses qualities that are much harder to manufacture.

It has a distinctive atmosphere. It understands the emotional importance of music. It creates a setting that feels worth saving. Most importantly, it recognizes that the people who surround us during formative years can become inseparable from our memories of that time.

The movie also understands something that many coming-of-age stories overlook: growing up isn’t just about leaving childhood behind. It’s about discovering which parts of yourself you want to keep.

The characters don’t need to abandon their individuality to become responsible. They don’t need to stop loving music, making mistakes, or spending time with people who understand them. They need to learn how to take themselves and one another seriously without losing the qualities that make them interesting.

Empire Records becomes a symbol of that possibility. It represents a space where individuality isn’t merely tolerated but celebrated, where people with different ambitions and personalities can share a common purpose.

That message helps explain why the film has endured despite its rocky initial reception.

The audience doesn’t return because every scene is perfect. It returns because the movie offers something emotionally recognizable: the feeling of finding a place where you belong, surrounded by people who make an otherwise ordinary day feel important.

For some viewers, that place was a record store. For others, it was a video rental shop, a local music venue, a favorite bar, a school hallway, or the living room where friends gathered to listen to albums and talk about everything that mattered.

The setting changes, but the feeling remains.

reminds us that some of the most important experiences in life happen in places that look unremarkable to everyone else. The people inside those places understand their significance because they have built something there together.

They have shared jokes, music, arguments, disappointments, and moments of unexpected kindness. They have created memories without realizing that those memories might eventually become the things they treasure most.

That’s the secret behind the movie’s lasting appeal.

It isn’t really about saving a record store. It’s about saving a little corner of the world where a group of young people can be themselves while they figure out what being themselves actually means.

And maybe that’s why continues to resonate decades after its release.

The world moves on. Businesses close. Music changes. People grow up and go their separate ways.

But somewhere in the back of our minds, we still remember the places where we felt like we belonged, the friends who made us laugh, and the songs that seemed to understand us better than anyone else.

captures that feeling beautifully.

Damn the man. Save the Empire.

items.title: Forgotten Band: Helmet
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are bands that disappear because they weren’t very good. There are bands that disappear because they had one hit and then vanished. And then there are bands like Helmet, who somehow managed to influence an enormous number of musicians, score a genuine alternative-rock hit, make several excellent albums and still end up feeling like a forgotten piece of the 1990s.

Helmet were never completely forgotten. Anyone who spent time digging through alternative metal, post-hardcore or ’90s heavy music knows exactly who they are. But compared with the influence they had, their place in popular music history is strangely small.

And that’s a shame because Helmet didn’t sound like anybody else.

They were heavy without being traditional metal. They were aggressive without relying on speed. They were technically sharp without sounding like a bunch of musicians showing off. Their riffs were brutally simple, but somehow incredibly difficult to duplicate.

At the center of it all was guitarist and singer Page Hamilton, whose dry, almost detached vocal style was the perfect match for the band’s enormous guitar sound.

Helmet didn’t need to scream constantly.

The riffs did enough screaming for them.

New York Before Alternative Metal

Helmet formed in New York City in 1989, with Hamilton joined by bassist Henry Bogdan and drummer John Stanier.

From the beginning, they occupied an interesting space between underground punk, hardcore and heavy metal.

They didn’t have the traditional look of a metal band.

There were no leather pants.

No guitar solos that lasted six minutes.

No interest in becoming the next arena-rock sensation.

Instead, Helmet built songs around heavy, repetitive guitar riffs and unusual rhythmic patterns.

The result was music that could sound almost mechanical.

Then it would suddenly explode.

Their early work attracted attention from the underground scene, eventually leading to a deal with Amphetamine Reptile Records.

Their debut album, , arrived in 1990 and immediately established the band’s identity.

It was abrasive, strange and ridiculously heavy.

But there was something else happening underneath the noise.

Changes Everything

Helmet’s breakthrough came with in 1992.

This is the album that should be mentioned whenever someone talks about the development of alternative metal.

It was heavy enough for metal fans, weird enough for alternative audiences and rhythmic enough to appeal to people who didn’t normally listen to either.

The production was cleaner than their debut, but Helmet never lost the unpleasant edge that made them interesting.

The riffs sounded like machinery.

The drums were incredibly tight.

And Page Hamilton’s vocals remained almost conversational.

That song gave Helmet their biggest mainstream exposure.

The guitar riff is deceptively simple.

It doesn’t sound complicated.

But try playing it properly.

Suddenly it becomes obvious why Helmet was different.

The rhythm is everything.

Helmet understood that a heavy riff doesn’t have to be fast.

It just has to hit at exactly the right moment.

They Were Never Really Grunge

This is where Helmet’s history gets interesting.

They arrived during the grunge explosion, but they didn’t really belong to it.

They were from New York rather than Seattle.

They weren’t particularly interested in the bluesy side of alternative rock.

They didn’t sound like Nirvana.

They didn’t sound like Pearl Jam.

They didn’t sound like Soundgarden.

Helmet were building something much more angular and mathematical.

The band became associated with the broader alternative-rock movement because that’s where the record stores and radio stations put them.

But their music pointed somewhere else.

You can hear pieces of Helmet’s sound in the alternative metal and nu-metal explosion that followed.

Bands began combining heavy riffs with hip-hop rhythms, industrial textures and unconventional song structures.

Helmet had already been doing something similar without needing to call it anything.

Was a Weird Left Turn

After the success of , Helmet could have easily made another version of the same album.

Released in 1994, was less straightforward and more experimental.

There were still enormous riffs, but Hamilton and the band were clearly interested in stretching their sound.

The arrangements became more unpredictable.

The album even incorporated unexpected influences and textures.

It wasn’t the obvious commercial follow-up.

That’s probably one reason Helmet never became a massive mainstream band.

They weren’t particularly interested in giving listeners exactly what they expected.

Helmet also became one of those bands whose music seemed to turn up everywhere during the 1990s.

Their songs appeared in movies and soundtracks, helping expose them to people who might never have bought a Helmet album.

They also contributed to the increasingly blurred boundary between alternative rock, metal and mainstream entertainment.

For a while, it seemed like Helmet might finally become a major rock act.

But they never quite made that leap.

And eventually, the band’s original run came to an end.

By that point, the alternative-rock landscape had changed dramatically.

The musical world that had embraced Helmet was moving toward nu-metal, pop punk and increasingly polished commercial rock.

The band’s influence remained obvious, but their own commercial momentum had slowed.

Hamilton eventually revived Helmet in the early 2000s with new musicians.

The band has continued through various lineups ever since.

That’s another reason the “forgotten band” label doesn’t quite fit.

They just stopped being part of the mainstream conversation.

The Bands They Influenced Became Bigger

This may be Helmet’s most frustrating legacy.

You can hear their influence in countless heavy alternative bands.

Their rhythmic approach became particularly important.

Instead of simply hammering away at power chords, Helmet treated the guitar almost like a percussion instrument.

The riffs locked into the drums.

The bass reinforced the groove.

Everything had to fit together.

That approach became hugely influential on alternative metal and later heavy music.

Helmet helped demonstrate that you could make music brutally heavy without playing at ridiculous speeds.

In the early 1990s, it wasn’t.

Why Did We Forget Helmet?

Because they were never particularly easy to categorize.

They were too heavy for alternative rock.

Too experimental for mainstream metal.

Too controlled for hardcore.

And just as they were becoming commercially successful, the musical landscape was changing underneath them.

That’s the unfortunate timing of Helmet.

If had arrived a few years later, perhaps the alternative-metal explosion would have made them enormous.

If it had arrived a few years earlier, they might have been remembered as pioneers of the underground metal scene.

Instead, they landed in the middle.

They became influential without becoming iconic.

They Deserve Another Look

If you’ve forgotten Helmet, is the obvious place to start.

Then go back to and move forward through .

What becomes immediately apparent is how modern some of this music still sounds.

The songwriting is tight without being predictable.

And Hamilton’s voice gives everything a strange sense of restraint.

Helmet didn’t need to scream at you to convince you they were heavy.

They simply turned up the amplifier and dropped the riff.

Just some of the most precise and punishing guitar music to come out of the American alternative scene.

Helmet aren’t really a forgotten band.

They’re a band whose influence is remembered more than the band itself.

People remember the sound.

They remember that Helmet was important.

But they don’t always go back and listen.

And that’s where they’re missing out.

Because isn’t just a relic from the early ’90s.

It’s still a monster of an album.

Helmet helped build the road that alternative metal traveled down during the next decade, and plenty of bigger bands drove straight past them on it.

Maybe it’s time to pull over and give the guys who built the road a little credit.

Helmet didn’t need to be the biggest band of the ’90s.

They just needed to be one of the heaviest.
